packet.headline_seed: Fired hacker twins forget to end Teams recording, capture own crimes
packet.description_seed: Perhaps you remember Muneeb and Sohaib Akhter, the 34-year-old twin brothers we profiled earlier this week . Although they had the tech chops to commit years of petty crimes (like stealing airline miles), what landed them in truly serious trouble was deleting 96 US government databases in the hour after both were fired last year by the same federal IT contractor, Opexus. (Opexus had just found out that both brothers had previously been in prison for cyberfraud.) The pair come off less as cybercriminal masterminds than as galumphing galoots —that is to say, a pair of bumbling oafs who thought that asking AI how to cover their tracks was going to keep them out of federal prison. One of the minor mysteries I encountered while writing the piece was that the government had a verbatim transcript of everything the brothers said to each other during their hour-long deletion spree. The two men lived together in Arlington, Virginia, so it made sense that they might be chatting in the same room rather than by text or instant message. But how the heck had the government gotten access to the audio? Supersecret software bugging? Crazy corporate spyware running on their company laptops? FBI agent in the bushes with a microphone? On February 18, 2025, two human resources (HR) employees of Company-1 [Opexus] scheduled a Microsoft Teams meeting with Sohaib and Muneeb. Sohaib recorded the meeting starting at 4:48pm Eastern Standard Time. The HR personnel left the meeting approximately 2 minutes and 40 seconds into the recording. Apparently unbeknownst to the defendants, the meeting continued recording the next hour of interactions between the brothers. And what did the pair discuss? Fortunately, this obscure document gives us a much fuller picture. If you’ve ever wondered what it sounds like to be in the room while cybercriminals do their thing, it sounds something like this: SOHA

original_article.research:
[Lähde: Ars Technica]
Perhaps you remember Muneeb and Sohaib Akhter, the 34-year-old twin brothers we profiled earlier this week. Although they had the tech chops to commit years of petty crimes (like stealing airline miles), what landed them in truly serious trouble was deleting 96 US government databases in the hour after both were fired last year by the same federal IT contractor, Opexus. (Opexus had just found out that both brothers had previously been in prison for cyberfraud.)

The pair come off less as cybercriminal masterminds than as galumphing galoots—that is to say, a pair of bumbling oafs who thought that asking AI how to cover their tracks was going to keep them out of federal prison.

One of the minor mysteries I encountered while writing the piece was that the government had a verbatim transcript of everything the brothers said to each other during their hour-long deletion spree. The two men lived together in Arlington, Virginia, so it made sense that they might be chatting in the same room rather than by text or instant message. But how the heck had the government gotten access to the audio? Supersecret software bugging? Crazy corporate spyware running on their company laptops? FBI agent in the bushes with a microphone?

I couldn’t figure it out, and the answer didn’t appear in any of the court documents I read. But a helpful source today pointed me to the answer. It is contained within a court filing that bears the unpropitious name, “UNITED STATES’ RESPONSE IN OPPOSITION TO DEFENDANT’S MOTION TO REVOKE THE DETENTION ORDER.”

This is the kind of title that practically begs you not to read its contents. Yet the file turns out to be fascinating. And it reveals that our galumphing galoots were supersecretly recorded by… themselves.

Because they forgot to stop recording the Teams meeting in which they were fired.

On February 18, 2025, two human resources (HR) employees of Company-1 [Opexus] scheduled a Microsoft Teams meeting with Sohaib and Muneeb. Sohaib recorded the meeting starting at 4:48pm Eastern Standard Time. The HR personnel left the meeting approximately 2 minutes and 40 seconds into the recording. Apparently unbeknownst to the defendants, the meeting continued recording the next hour of interactions between the brothers.

And what did the pair discuss? Fortunately, this obscure document gives us a much fuller picture. If you’ve ever wondered what it sounds like to be in the room while cybercriminals do their thing, it sounds something like this:

payload.title: Irtisanotut kaksoset tallensivat vahingossa oman tietomurtoepäilynsä Teamsiin
payload.summary: Yhdysvalloissa kaksosveljesten epäilty tietojen poistaminen tallentui Microsoft Teams -kokouksen nauhoitukselle sen jälkeen, kun henkilöstöhallinnon työntekijät olivat poistuneet irtisanomiskeskustelusta.
payload.content:
Yhdysvalloissa Muneeb ja Sohaib Akhterin, 34-vuotiaiden kaksosveljesten, epäilty tunnin mittainen tietojen poistaminen tallentui Microsoft Teams -kokouksen nauhoitukselle sen jälkeen, kun heidät oli irtisanottu liittovaltion IT-urakoitsija Opexuksesta helmikuussa 2025. Tapaus on poikkeuksellinen, koska viranomaisilla oli käytössään sanatarkka aineisto siitä, mitä veljekset puhuivat keskenään väitetyn poistamisen aikana.

## Irtisanomiskokous jäi käyntiin

Tapahtumat alkoivat 18. helmikuuta 2025, kun kaksi henkilöstöhallinnon työntekijää järjesti Microsoft Teams -kokouksen Sohaib ja Muneeb Akhterin kanssa. Sohaib aloitti kokouksen tallennuksen kello 16.48 paikallista itärannikon aikaa.

Henkilöstöhallinnon työntekijät poistuivat kokouksesta noin kahden minuutin ja 40 sekunnin kuluttua tallennuksen alusta. Käytettävissä olevan aineiston mukaan veljekset eivät ilmeisesti huomanneet, että kokous ja sen tallennus jatkuivat heidän välisensä keskustelun ajan.

Juuri tämä yksityiskohta selittää, miksi viranomaisilla oli käytössään sanatarkka jäljennös siitä, mitä veljekset sanoivat toisilleen seuraavan noin tunnin aikana. Veljekset asuivat Arlingtonissa Virginiassa, joten heidän on arvioitu voineen keskustella samassa tilassa ilman viestipalveluita.

## Epäilty poistaminen koski 96 tietokantaa

Veljekset joutuivat vakaviin vaikeuksiin, koska heidän epäillään poistaneen 96 Yhdysvaltain hallinnon tietokantaa tunnin sisällä siitä, kun molemmat oli irtisanottu Opexuksesta. Yhtiö oli juuri saanut tietää, että veljekset olivat aiemmin olleet vankilassa kyberpetoksista.

Aineiston perusteella tapaus ei näyttäydy erityisen huolellisesti suunniteltuna operaationa. Veljeksillä kuvataan olleen teknistä osaamista myös aiempiin vähäisempiin rikoksiin, kuten lentomailien varastamiseen, mutta tällä kertaa keskeinen ongelma oli se, että heidän omat keskustelunsa jäivät talteen.

Tapauksessa on myös erikoinen tekoälyyn liittyvä piirre: veljesten kerrotaan pohtineen tekoälyn käyttämistä jälkien peittämiseen. Se ei kuitenkaan estänyt tutkijoita saamasta käsitystä tapahtumien kulusta, koska Teams-tallenne oli jäänyt päälle juuri kriittiseksi ajaksi.

Kokonaisuutena tapaus korostaa, kuinka tavallinen työpaikkaviestinnän työkalu voi muodostua ratkaisevaksi todisteeksi kyberrikosepäilyssä. Samalla se muistuttaa, että irtisanomistilanteisiin liittyvät käyttöoikeudet ja järjestelmäpääsyt ovat organisaatioille erityisen riskialtis hetki.

Veljesten epäillään poistaneen 96 Yhdysvaltain hallinnon tietokantaa irtisanomisensa jälkeen.
Tallenne jäi päälle sen jälkeen, kun henkilöstöhallinnon työntekijät olivat poistuneet kokouksesta.

article.description: Yhdysvalloissa kaksosveljesten epäilty tietojen poistaminen tallentui Microsoft Teams -kokouksen nauhoitukselle sen jälkeen, kun henkilöstöhallinnon työntekijät olivat poistuneet irtisanomiskeskustelusta.
article.research:
[Lähde: Ars Technica]
Perhaps you remember Muneeb and Sohaib Akhter, the 34-year-old twin brothers we profiled earlier this week. Although they had the tech chops to commit years of petty crimes (like stealing airline miles), what landed them in truly serious trouble was deleting 96 US government databases in the hour after both were fired last year by the same federal IT contractor, Opexus. (Opexus had just found out that both brothers had previously been in prison for cyberfraud.)

The pair come off less as cybercriminal masterminds than as galumphing galoots—that is to say, a pair of bumbling oafs who thought that asking AI how to cover their tracks was going to keep them out of federal prison.

One of the minor mysteries I encountered while writing the piece was that the government had a verbatim transcript of everything the brothers said to each other during their hour-long deletion spree. The two men lived together in Arlington, Virginia, so it made sense that they might be chatting in the same room rather than by text or instant message. But how the heck had the government gotten access to the audio? Supersecret software bugging? Crazy corporate spyware running on their company laptops? FBI agent in the bushes with a microphone?

I couldn’t figure it out, and the answer didn’t appear in any of the court documents I read. But a helpful source today pointed me to the answer. It is contained within a court filing that bears the unpropitious name, “UNITED STATES’ RESPONSE IN OPPOSITION TO DEFENDANT’S MOTION TO REVOKE THE DETENTION ORDER.”

This is the kind of title that practically begs you not to read its contents. Yet the file turns out to be fascinating. And it reveals that our galumphing galoots were supersecretly recorded by… themselves.

Because they forgot to stop recording the Teams meeting in which they were fired.

Sohaib recorded the meeting starting at 4:48pm Eastern Standard Time. The HR personnel left the meeting approximately 2 minutes and 40 seconds into the recording. Apparently unbeknownst to the defendants, the meeting continued recording the next hour of interactions between the brothers.

And what did the pair discuss? Fortunately, this obscure document gives us a much fuller picture. If you’ve ever wondered what it sounds like to be in the room while cybercriminals do their thing, it sounds something like this:

The pair come off less as cybercriminal masterminds than as galumphing galoots—that is to say, a pair of bumbling oafs who thought that asking AI how to cover their tracks was going to keep them out of federal prison.

One of the minor mysteries I encountered while writing the piece was that the government had a verbatim transcript of everything the brothers said to each other during their hour-long deletion spree. The two men lived together in Arlington, Virginia, so it made sense that they might be chatting in the same room rather than by text or instant message. But how the heck had the government gotten access to the audio? Supersecret software bugging? Crazy corporate spyware running on their company laptops? FBI agent in the bushes with a microphone?

On February 18, 2025, two human resources (HR) employees of Company-1 [Opexus] scheduled a Microsoft Teams meeting with Sohaib and Muneeb. Sohaib recorded the meeting starting at 4:48pm Eastern Standard Time. The HR personnel left the meeting approximately 2 minutes and 40 seconds into the recording. Apparently unbeknownst to the defendants, the meeting continued recording the next hour of interactions between the brothers. And what did the pair discuss? Fortunately, this obscure document gives us a much fuller picture. If you’ve ever wondered what it sounds like to be in the room while cybercriminals do their thing, it sounds something like this: SOHA
